analysis.one_liner: Requires offshore oil and gas lease sales off Virginia, with half the royalties shared with the state.
analysis.headline: The bill to require federal oil and gas lease sales off Virginia's coast never received a committee vote and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced the Interior Department to hold oil and gas lease auctions off Virginia's coast, including a specific sale known as Lease Sale 220. Half of the money the government collects from those leases — rents, royalties, and bonus bids — would go to the U.S. Treasury's general fund, and half to a special account for Virginia, with most of Virginia's share going to the state and the rest spent on conservation, public transit, and alternative energy. The President could block any tract that interfered with military operations. The bill also would have redrawn the federal map of the mid-Atlantic leasing area so each state's share of leasable waters matched the length of its tidal shoreline.
analysis.who_benefits: Virginia's state government would gain a new, dedicated revenue stream from federal waters — roughly 37.5 cents of every royalty dollar, with a quarter of that earmarked for land and water conservation, public transit, and alternative energy projects. Oil and gas companies would gain access to new federal leases off the Atlantic coast. Nationally, drilling supporters argued it would add domestic energy supply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Virginia's treasury and oil and gas companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Interior Secretary to include Lease Sale 220 and revised mid-Atlantic areas in the fiscal 2012-2017 offshore leasing program, guaranteeing the sales would be scheduled rather than left to the administration's discretion.

Half of all lease revenues would be deposited in a Treasury account for Virginia: 75 percent disbursed directly to the state, and 25 percent spent at the President's discretion on state land and water conservation, public transportation, and alternative energy systems.
Tracts could not be leased where the President determines a lease would conflict with military operations relating to national security, protecting areas used by the Navy.

The bill would redraw the mid-Atlantic leasing map so the leasable area is proportional to each state's tidal shoreline, using a 1975 NOAA shoreline document — a change affecting how waters off Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina are allocated.

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities, commercial fisheries, and tourism businesses would bear the risk of spills and drilling disruption off their shores, with no dedicated compensation fund in the bill. The federal Treasury would give up a larger share of royalties than it keeps under standard offshore law, spreading the cost across all federal taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coastal fisheries, tourism, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Opening the mid-Atlantic outer Continental Shelf to drilling exposes coastal fisheries, beaches, and tourism economies to spill and discharge risk, and the bill contains no dedicated liability or compensation provisions beyond existing law.
By mandating the lease sales in statute, the bill locks in fossil fuel development in the mid-Atlantic planning area for the 2012-2017 program regardless of future administrations' preferences.

The map revision would change which waters each mid-Atlantic state can claim benefits from, effectively reallocating the leasable area among Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina by shoreline length rather than the 2010 boundaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The revenue-sharing design is unusually generous to the state — Virginia would keep a larger cut of federal royalties than coastal states typically receive — and the military carve-out and transit and conservation earmarks show real attention to state priorities. But the environmental risk falls on a narrow group (coastal fishing and tourism interests) while the money flows broadly, and the bill does nothing to expand drilling-safety requirements or compensation for spill damages. Whether the trade is worth it depends heavily on how much oil is actually off Virginia, which the bill does not address.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Webb introduced the bill on July 6, 2011, on behalf of himself and Sen. Mark Warner, both Virginia Democrats.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day, which was the only action it ever received.
No committee markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action appears in the record before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the waters off Virginia stayed unleased during the 112th Congress: oil and gas companies did not gain the lease access the bill would have guaranteed, and coastal fishing and tourism interests were not exposed to the drilling risk it would have created. Virginians also did not receive the royalty stream it promised.

for.name: Sen. Jim Webb
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to mandate offshore lease sales off Virginia and share royalties with the state.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or vote.

against.name: Jeff Bingaman
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee during the 112th Congress and never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists; its only supporters on record were two Virginia Democrats, and the provided sources show no recorded opposition or cosponsorship from the other party.

industries.note: The bill guarantees the industry access to new federal lease auctions off Virginia, converting public seabed into private drilling rights. Its gain comes with spill and pollution risk borne by nearby coastal communities rather than by the lessees themselves, beyond existing liability law.

Drilling platforms and any spill off the mid-Atlantic coast would directly threaten the waters, catches, and beaches these businesses depend on, and the bill offers them no dedicated protection or compensation.
The state would receive a permanent 37.5 percent share of all lease revenues, funding conservation, transit, and alternative energy — a direct fiscal gain for the state's budget and residents.
The bill overrides the standard offshore revenue formula, directing half of all royalties to Virginia instead of the general fund, reducing the federal share relative to ordinary offshore law.
